Enhancing semi-continuous anaerobic digestion efficiency with nanobubble 
water: thermophysical properties optimization and microbial regulation
Yongkang Yuan a,b, Tingting Hou a,b, Pengfei Li a,b, Hui Sun a,b, Youzhou Jiao a,b,c, Gang Li a,b,  
Chao He a,b,*
a Key Laboratory of New Materials and Facilities for Rural Renewable Energy of Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs, College of Mechanical & Electrical Engineering, 
Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou, 450002, China
b Henan International Joint Laboratory of Biomass Energy and Nanomaterials, Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou, 450002, China
c Henan University of Engineering, Zhengzhou, 451191, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Nanobubble water
Semi-continuous
Anaerobic digestion
Thermophysical properties
Microbial communities
A B S T R A C T
The utilization of nanobubbles to enhance biomass anaerobic digestion (AD) for bioenergy production has 
emerged as a prominent research focus. However, the mechanisms governing their effects on semi-continuous AD 
characteristics and heat-mass transfer processes remain inadequately elucidated. This research employed corn 
stover as feedstock for semi-continuous AD at 35 ± 1 ◦C, investigating the impacts of nanobubble water (NBW) 
prepared with H2, CH4, and CO2 on digestion performance, thermophysical properties (thermal conductivity, 
specific heat capacity, density, viscosity, surface tension), and microbial dynamics. The results demonstrated that 
NBW-supplemented systems achieved up to 15.67 ± 1.96 % higher daily methane production compared to the 
control. Compared to the control group, NBW-supplemented systems demonstrated improvements of 7.22–29.50 
% and 5.06–18.85 % in total solids and volatile solids removal efficiencies, respectively. Concurrently, soluble 
chemical oxygen demand and reducing sugar concentrations decreased by 7.36–13.07 % and 3.34–10.61 % in 
NBW groups. NBW enhanced mass transfer efficiency, thereby inducing selective microbial enrichment and 
functional augmentation that improved substrate utilization. Furthermore, NBW optimized digestate thermal 
stability and flow properties, consequently enhancing heat-mass transfer efficiency during AD. This work elu­
cidates nanobubble-mediated enhancement mechanisms in semi-continuous AD through integrated thermo­
physical and microbiological perspectives, thus providing a theoretical foundation for advanced biogas 
production technologies.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) serves as a critical technology for valo­
rizing organic wastes, holding substantial practical significance in 
renewable energy development and environmental protection. The AD 
process fundamentally relies on microbial metabolic systems, through 
which complex organic matter is biochemically converted into value- 
added products, including methane and short-chain fatty acids [1]. 
However, conventional AD occurs within complex fluid systems where 
low mass transfer efficiency and slow reaction kinetics persist as 
pervasive challenges [2].
Nanobubbles (NBs) demonstrate significant potential in AD appli­
cations due to their distinctive physicochemical properties, including 
large specific surface area, negative zeta potential, radical generation 
capacity, and enhanced mass transfer rates [3]. The extremely small 
dimensions of NBs confer exceptional longevity in aqueous environ­
ments, thereby prolonging gas-liquid interfacial mass transfer processes 
and achieving superior mass transfer efficiency. For instance, CO2 NBs 
exhibited 11-fold higher mass transfer coefficients and 7-fold greater 
buffering capacity compared to conventional CO2 macrobubbles [4]. 
Numerous studies confirm that NBs enhance microbial and enzymatic 
activities while promoting substrate degradation, consequently 
improving AD efficiency [5]. However, NBs have a limited lifespan, and 
their effectiveness may gradually decline during long-term AD pro­
cesses. Furthermore, existing studies on NB-enhanced AD have pre­
dominantly been conducted in batch-fed reactor systems, with limited

research carried out under semi-continuous operation [6,7]. In 
semi-continuous systems, frequent feeding and discharge operations, 
along with variations in operational cycles, may influence the actual 
performance of NBs. Therefore, incorporating NBs into semi-continuous 
AD processes is of significant importance for advancing their engineer­
ing application in the field of AD. H2 and CO2 act as key substrates for 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens and play essential roles in the metabolic 
pathways of AD systems [8]. Meanwhile, H2, CO2, and CH4 are the 
primary components of biogas. A systematic investigation of these three 
gases will also provide valuable insights for the subsequent development 
of biogas-nanobubble water (biogas-NBW).
In AD systems, the thermophysical properties of digestate directly 
influence heat and mass transfer efficiencies within reactors. The ther­
mophysical properties of digestate mainly include density, viscosity, 
surface tension, thermal conductivity, and specific heat capacity, which 
are influenced by the composition of the substance, substrate concen­
tration, temperature, microbial metabolites, and other aspects [9,10]. 
Density, viscosity, and surface tension collectively determine rheolog­
ical behavior, thereby affecting mass transfer rates. For instance, 
elevated substrate concentrations increase digestate viscosity, impairing 
fluidity [11]. Reduced surface tension enhances molecular diffusion, 
consequently improving mass transfer efficiency. Critically, diminished 
surface tension correlates with accelerated organic degradation and 
biogas production [12]. Thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity 
define heat transfer characteristics, jointly regulating thermal energy 
transport and temperature distribution. Studies have confirmed that 
higher total solids (TS) concentrations decrease specific heat capacity in 
pulp substrates [13]. Compared to pure water, the total heat transfer 
coefficient of the reactor decreased by 49.51 % when the digestate was 
used as a fluid [14]. Therefore, the thermophysical properties of the 
digestate can directly affect the matter and energy transfer in the system. 
The poor thermophysical properties increase the resistance to thermal 
mass transfer and impact the growth and metabolism of microorgan­
isms, which is the current challenge of AD.
The superior gas-liquid mass transfer efficiency of NBs inherently 
induces thermophysical modifications in digestate. Current research 
predominantly focuses on NBs impacts on AD end-products, while sys­
tematic investigations into their effects on digestate thermophysical 
properties remain underexplored. Some studies have currently explored 
the physicochemical properties of single liquid-phase systems of NBW 
through simulations. For example, when different dimensions and 
numbers of NBs burst, there were different density and temperature 
variations in their regions [15]. In addition, some calculations found 
that the presence of N2, CO2, and O2 NBs increased the specific heat 
capacity of dodecane and isooctane [16]. However, the influence reg­
ularities of NBW on the thermophysical properties of the complex 
liquid-phase system of digestate needs to be supplemented.
In this research, the effects of NBW with different gas species on the 
properties of corn stalk semi-continuous AD and the thermophysical 
properties of digestate were investigated experimentally. The research 
specifically examines: (1) impacts of various NBW types on methane 
production and substrate degradation efficiency; (2) modifications of 
digestate density, viscosity, surface tension, thermal conductivity, and 
specific heat capacity during semi-continuous operation; (3) microbial 
community restructuring and functional gene expression alterations 
induced by NBW supplementation. The findings provide critical tech­
nical parameters for designing and optimizing NBW-coupled AD sys­
tems, advancing technological upgrading of high-efficiency biogas 
production platforms.
2. Methods
2.1. Preparation of raw materials
The experiment used corn stalks as the substrate for digestion and 
activated sludge as the inoculum. The raw material characteristics are 
shown in Table 1. Corn stalks were obtained from the Xuchang experi­
mental field of Henan Agricultural University, crushed and sieved 
through a 60-mesh sieve. The activated sludge was collected from the 
Zhengzhou Matougang wastewater treatment plant and activated for 
two weeks at 35 ◦C in an incubator before use. A cavitation nanobubble 
generator (ZJC-NM-200L, ZJ Environmental Protection, China) was 
used to prepare NBW with a gas flow rate of 50 mL/min and a NBW flow 
rate of 3 L/min, employing a circular method (volume 2 L, duration 5 
min). The experiments employed the three primary components of 
biogas (H2, CH4, and CO2) as carrier gases, producing H2-NBW, CH4- 
NBW, and CO2-NBW, respectively.
2.2. Experimental protocol and device
The experiment employed a continuous stirred tank reactor (CSTR) 
with a total volume of 4.4 L and a working volume of 3 L (Fig. 1). The 
feedstock was introduced into the reactor through the feed inlet and 
underwent AD. The digested effluent was discharged from the effluent 
outlet, while the residual sludge was expelled from the sludge discharge 
port located at the bottom of the reactor. The four equally sized CSTR AD 
reactors were named A1, A2, A3, and A4. A1-A4 used deionized water, 
H2-NBW, CH4-NBW, and CO2-NBW, respectively. AD was conducted in 
semi-continuous operation with 14 days start-up period. During the 
start-up phase, NBW would be mixed with sludge and corn stalks before 
being poured into the reactor for anaerobic digestion. Started with small 
amounts of substrate and began semi-continuous operation after the 
methane concentration stabilized. During the semi-continuous opera­
tion phase, after daily efflux, an equal volume of NBW and substrate 
mixture was added to the reactor. The hydraulic retention time (HRT) 
and sludge retention time (SRT) for semi-continuous operation were 
both 15 days, and the volumetric loading rate (VLR) was 2 gVS/(L⋅d). 
The stirring frequency was 6 times/day, 15 min/time.
2.3. Analytical instruments and methods
Methane concentration was determined using a gas chromatograph 
(6820 GC, Agilent, USA) equipped with a 5A molecular sieve packed 
column and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). Nitrogen was used as 
the carrier gas at a flow rate of 45 mL/min. The oven temperature was 
set at 80 ◦C, while the detector and injector temperatures were main­
tained at 150 ◦C and 100 ◦C, respectively. The pH value was measured 
with a pH meter (PHS-3E, Leici, China). Total solids (TS) content was 
determined by drying the samples in an oven (101, Zhongxing, China) at 
105 ◦C until a constant weight was achieved. Volatile solids (VS) content 
was measured by combusting dried samples in a muffle furnace (MF- 
2200, Chuangxin Instrument, China) at 600 ◦C for 3 h. The volatile fatty 
acid (VFA) concentration was analyzed using a gas chromatograph 
(7890B, Agilent, USA) equipped with a DB-FFAP column and a flame 
ionization detector (FID). Nitrogen was employed as the carrier gas at a 
flow rate of 30 mL/min. The column temperature was set at 230 ◦C, and 
both the injector and detector temperatures were maintained at 250 ◦C. 
Reducing sugars were determined via the anthrone colorimetric method, 
and soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) was measured by the 
potassium dichromate spectrophotometric method [17,18].
The density of the digestate was determined using a density meter

(Alpha-s, Guangzhou Beto, China) employing the pendant drop method 
[20]. Specific heat capacity was measured using a simultaneous thermal 
analyzer (SDT650, TA Instruments, USA) under a nitrogen atmosphere

nuclear magnetic resonance imaging system (MesoMR23-060H-I, Niu­
mag, China). All measurements were performed in triplicate to minimize 
experimental error.
2.4. Microbiological analyses
Microbial samples were collected from the original microorganisms 
(OM) and terminal microbial communities of semi-continuous AD 
groups (CG: control group; H-NBW: H2-NBW; CH4-NBW; M-NBW; C- 
NBW: CO2-NBW). Microbial community structure and functional genes 
were detected using high-throughput sequencing by Sangon Biotech Co., 
Ltd. (Shanghai, China). DNA extraction was performed using the E.Z.N. 
A™ Mag-Bind Soil DNA Kit (Omega, M5635-02, USA). Bacterial 
amplification targeted the V3-V4 hypervariable regions using primers 
341F/805R. Archaeal communities were analyzed through nested PCR 
amplification. The first-round amplification was performed using 
primers 340F and 1000R, followed by secondary amplification with 
primers 349F and 806R, targeting the V3-V4 hypervariable regions of 
the 16S rRNA gene. Library quality was verified by 2 % agarose gel 
electrophoresis prior to sequencing on the Illumina NextSeq 2000 
platform (Illumina, USA). PICRUSt (v1.1.4) and FAPROTAX (v1.2.1) 
were used for annotation of 16S rRNA gene sequencing data to predict 
microbial metabolic functions.
2.5. Energy conversion efficiency analysis
The energy conversion efficiency assessment was calculated using 
the following equation:

NBW flow rate (3 L/min). 
Wcir = We⋅(Q ⋅tcir / Vcir)
(Eq. 2) 
where Wcir is the energy consumed in the circulation preparation of 1 L 
of NBW (J/L), tcir is the circulation time (5 min), and Vcir is the circu­
lation volume (2 L). 
Vn = Vo(1 −Rinoc) / Ve
(Eq. 3) 
where Vn is the volume of NBW required per unit volume of the reactor 
(L/L), Vo is the output volume (0.20 L), Rinoc is the inoculum ratio (0.30), 
and Ve is the effective volume of the reactor (3 L). 
Wctrl = QCH4⋅Vctrl

(kJ/L), QCH4 is the lower heating value of methane (803.49 kJ/mol), Vctrl 
is the volumetric methane production of the control group (L/L), and Vm

compared to the control group (dimensionless).
2.6. Data processing and analyses
All experimental datasets were processed and statistically analyzed 
using Microsoft Excel (v2016) for data organization and one-way 
ANOVA testing, with a statistical significance threshold established at 
p = 0.05. Origin (v2022) was employed for graphical analysis, where all 
data visualizations incorporated error bars representing the standard 
deviation to illustrate data dispersion.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Methane production
Daily methane yield first increased and then stabilized over time, 
achieving stability during the second HRT (Fig. 2a). Throughout the 
semi-continuous operation period, NBW-supplemented groups exhibited 
significantly higher methane yields than the control group (p < 0.05). 
During stable methanogenic operation (HRT 2–3), the NBW groups 
demonstrated 9.68 ± 2.08 % (H2-NBW), 7.34 ± 2.07 % (CH4-NBW), and 
15.67 ± 1.96 % (CO2-NBW) increases in daily methane production 
compared to the control group (159.88 ± 2.34 mL/(gVS⋅d)). Cumulative 
methane yield in NBW groups increased by 11.71 ± 2.50 % (H2-NBW), 
9.92 ± 2.42 % (CH4-NBW), and 16.08 ± 2.45 % (CO2-NBW) compared 
to the control (37.90 ± 0.61 L total). Although different NBs exerted 
distinct effects on substrate degradation and microbial community 
composition, all demonstrated positive impacts on methanogenesis 
[21]. Notably, CO2-NBW achieved the highest daily methane yield and 
cumulative yield in semi-continuous AD compared to H2-NBW and 
CH4-NBW. The differential effects of identical gas-species NBW may 
arise from variations in bubble generation conditions and AD environ­
ments. For instance, H2-NBW demonstrated superior methanogenic 
enhancement in swine manure AD systems, whereas CO2-NBW showed

greater methane production performance in semi-continuous AD of rice 
straw substrates [22,23]. The superior performance of CO2-NBW in 
semi-continuous systems may relate to enhanced gas dissolution kinetics 
under continuous liquid-phase mixing.
The stimulatory effects of NBs gradually attenuated during pro­
longed operation (Fig. 2b). During the first HRT, cumulative methane 
production increased by 14.95 ± 2.86 % (H2-NBW), 15.45 ± 2.66 % 
(CH4-NBW), and 22.56 ± 2.86 % (CO2-NBW) compared to controls. 
These enhancements declined to 11.57 ± 2.84 %, 8.76 ± 2.71 %, and 
12.02 ± 2.94 % in the second HRT, further reducing to 9.68 ± 2.08 %, 
7.34 ± 2.07 %, and 15.67 ± 1.96 % in the third HRT. This deterioration 
likely resulted from reduced NBs persistence under continuous stirring 
and feeding-induced hydraulic shear forces. Lower pH conditions and 
elevated organic matter concentrations were found to significantly 
reduce NBs longevity, with persistence durations typically ranging be­
tween several days and weeks under such operational parameters [24]. 
Notably, methane concentration remained statistically indistinguishable 
between NBW groups and controls (p > 0.05, Fig. 2c). Similarly, 
N2-NBW increased methane production by 29 % in sludge AD, whereas 
methane concentration showed no statistically significant variation 
[25]. This phenomenon reflects the dynamic equilibrium between 
methanogenic and acidogenic rates. As demonstrated in previous 
research, NBs facilitated the disruption of oligosaccharide layers on 
cellulose surfaces, thereby enhancing the hydrolysis of lignocellulosic 
substrates [5]. However, the increased substrate availability concur­
rently elevates both biogas production and competitive gas generation 
(e.g., CO2/H2), ultimately maintaining stable methane concentration 
(Fig. S1).
3.2. Substrate degradation
3.2.1. pH, VFAs concentration and TS/VS removal rates
The pH initially increased, subsequently decreased, and then grad­
ually rose and stabilized (Fig. 2c). During system initiation, the higher 
pH of the fresh feedstock compared to reactor content caused transient 
pH elevation. Progressive substrate hydrolysis during continuous

feeding reduced system pH to 6.85 ± 0.05, coinciding with accelerated 
VFAs accumulation. Transition to methanogenic stability phase facili­
tated rapid VFAs consumption, driving pH recovery and stabilization at 
7.00 ± 0.05. CO2-NBW enhanced VFA turnover under moderate sub­
strate loading, though its buffering capacity diminished at extremes 
[26]. No significant pH variation (p > 0.05) was observed between NBW 
groups and the control, likely due to hydraulic shear forces and extended 
operational duration attenuating NB-mediated pH regulation.
The VFAs dynamics reflected the pH variations, with total VFAs 
concentrations in the NBW groups exceeding those of the control during 
the initial accumulation phase (0–16 days) (Fig. 2e). On day 16, the total 
VFAs concentrations in H2-NBW, CH4-NBW, and CO2-NBW increased by 
62.99 ± 9.34 %, 45.44 ± 5.01 %, and 14.00 ± 5.48 %, respectively, 
compared to the control group (128.60 ± 4.40 mg/L). This aligns with 
prior findings where CO2/Air-NBW enhanced VFAs production in cel­
lulose digestion through improved hydrolase activity [27].
NBW supplementation significantly improved substrate conversion 
efficiency, with H2-NBW, CH4-NBW, and CO2-NBW achieving 11.89 ±
2.56 %, 5.06 ± 2.33 %, and 18.85 ± 2.73 % increases in VS removal, 
and 7.22 ± 2.65 %, 11.24 ± 2.24 %, and 29.50 ± 2.22 % TS reduction 
versus control (Fig. 2d). Some research suggested that CO2-NBW sup­
plementation has been documented to enhance β-glucosidase activity, 
consequently improving TS and VS removal efficiencies [28]. The 
coupled phenomena of increased VFAs concentration and reduced solid 
content confirm that NBW can enhance the hydrolytic-acidogenic phase. 
Enhanced hydrolysis of corn stover under NBW treatment generated 
increased quantities of low-molecular-weight organic compounds, 
thereby significantly enhancing substrate utilization efficiency.
3.2.2. SCOD and reducing sugars
As illustrated in Fig. 3a, the SCOD exhibited an initial increase fol­
lowed by stabilization, primarily governed by the dynamics of substrate 
concentration within the reactor. The initial SCOD elevation resulted 
from feed-induced stimulation of hydrolytic microbial activity, thereby 
enhancing the release of soluble organic matter. Subsequently, a kinetic 
equilibrium was established among hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and 
methanogenesis processes. Hydrolysis products were sequentially con­
verted to VFAs, which were rapidly consumed for methanogenesis,

enhanced utilization of soluble substrates for microbial metabolism and 
growth. Similarly, the implementation of Air-NBs for wastewater aera­
tion demonstrated a substantial enhancement in COD removal effi­
ciency, increasing from 41.21 % (conventional bubble aeration) to 92.5 
% [29].
Reducing sugars, as primary hydrolysis products in lignocellulosic 
digestion, reflected substrate hydrolysis-acidification progression 
(Fig. 3b). Initial accumulation occurred when hydrolysis rates exceeded 
acidogenic consumption. System stabilization established a metabolic 
equilibrium where sugar generation and consumption rates converged. 
Compared to the control, the reducing sugar concentration in the NBW 
groups exhibited a 3.34–10.61 % reduction. This indicates that NBW 
supplementation accelerated the reducing sugar consumption rate, 
facilitating enhanced conversion to VFAs through the glycolytic 
pathway, consistent with the VFAs concentration dynamics (Fig. 2e). 
These observations align with prior findings in swine manure AD, where 
NBW not only increased substrate hydrolysis rates but also accelerated 
the consumption of soluble proteins and carbohydrates [23].
3.3. Thermophysical properties of digestate
3.3.1. Heat transfer properties
The digestate constitutes a multiphase system encompassing sus­
pended solids, soluble compounds, and biogas; these components 
differentially influence heat transfer characteristics based on their 
physicochemical properties. As illustrated in Fig. 3c, the thermal con­
ductivity of the digestate exhibited an initial decrease, followed by an 
increase and subsequent stabilization during semi-continuous operation, 
with overall values ranging from 0.09 to 0.14 W/(m⋅K). The early-phase 
reduction (days 0–9) correlated with transient substrate accumulation 
following feeding, which increased solid fraction content. Subsequently, 
enhanced microbial degradation converted particulate organics into 
soluble constituents, progressively elevating thermal conductivity. 
While higher moisture content generally increases thermal conductivity, 
elevated straw content reduces it due to porous biomass structure [30]. 
Notably, the presence of solid particulates occasionally resulted in 
conductivity exceeding that of pure water [31]. One-way ANOVA 
revealed no statistically significant intergroup differences (p = 0.95), 
indicating minimal NBW impact on digestate thermal conductivity.
Fig. 3d illustrates the gradual decrease and subsequent stabilization 
of digestate specific heat capacity during semi-continuous operation. 
Composed primarily of water, soluble organics, straw residues, and 
suspended solids, these constituents collectively determine the specific 
heat capacity. Due to the significantly higher specific heat capacity of 
water (4.18 kJ/(kg⋅K)), an increase in substrate concentration typically 
reduces the overall specific heat capacity of the digestate [32]. This 
trend is consistent with observations relating to soybean molasses 
wastewater, where the specific heat capacity was found to decrease 
progressively as the TS concentration increased [33]. During initial 
reactor operation, escalating substrate concentrations were correlated 
with a decline in specific heat capacity. Specific heat capacity quantifies 
the thermal energy required to alter the temperature of a material, 
indicating its susceptibility to external thermal perturbations. Lower 
specific heat values accelerate temperature response rates and amplify 
thermal fluctuations. The H2-NBW group exhibited the highest mean 
specific heat capacity (3.54 ± 0.07 kJ/(kg⋅K)), representing a 1.23 ±
0.33 % increase compared to the control (p < 0.05). This enhancement 
primarily stems from NBW-induced degradation of solid substrates into 
soluble fractions, which possess higher heat capacities. Thermal stability 
is critical for sustained AD performance. Consequently, NBW supple­
mentation enhances the thermodynamic resilience of the system by 
modulating heat capacity characteristics.
3.3.2. Density and rheological properties
In AD of straw biomass, digestate density is primarily determined by 
substrate concentration. Overall, the density demonstrated an initial 
decrease followed by a gradual increase and stabilization during semi- 
continuous operation (Fig. 3e). During the early operational phase 
(days 0–3), the discharge of accumulated non-degradable solids from the 
startup period led to a reduction in digestate density. Subsequently, 
continuous feeding progressively increased organic matter concentra­
tion within the reactor, elevating density until stabilization. This agrees 
with observations in dairy manure digestion, where higher TS content 
correlates with increased digestate density [34]. NBW-supplemented 
groups exhibited marginally lower densities than the control during 
the initial 3 days, subsequently showing slightly higher values. The 
early-phase density reduction in NBW systems resulted from the 
intrinsic lower density of NBW compared to deionized water. The 
addition of NBW promoted the release of soluble substrates, resulting in 
an increase in digestate density.
Liquid surface tension reflects the magnitude of intermolecular 
forces, with digestate surface tension being significantly influenced by 
soluble organic constituents [35]. As shown in Fig. 3f, surface tension 
exhibited a generally decreasing trend with periodic fluctuations 
throughout the semi-continuous AD process. The surface tension of 
digestate decreases as the concentration of soluble substrates increases. 
This inverse relationship is evidenced by a strongly negative Spearman 
correlation between surface tension and VFAs concentrations under 
long-chain fatty acid stress conditions [36]. During the early operation 
(days 0–15), escalating soluble organic content progressively reduced 
surface tension. The mid-phase (days 15–23) showed temporary tension 
elevation due to rapid VFAs consumption by accelerated methano­
genesis. Subsequently, the increased reducing sugars from cellulose/­
hemicellulose hydrolysis caused a slight reduction in tension in the final 
phase. Throughout the semi-continuous operation, digestate surface 
tension in NBW-supplemented groups remained consistently lower than 
in the control. Research suggests that NBs function as Janus-like parti­
cles, semi-hydrophilic semi-hydrophobic entities that weaken interfacial 
tension by disrupting hydrogen-bonding networks in water, conse­
quently reducing surface tension [37]. Concurrently, NBs stimulate the 
acidogenic phase, and the resultant elevation in VFAs concentration 
further diminishes digestate surface tension. The attenuation effect 
weakened during later operation due to a decrease in NBs concentration. 
Mean surface tension values were quantified as 71.49 ± 0.70 mN/m 
(H2-NBW), 71.43 ± 0.45 mN/m (CH4-NBW), and 71.83 ± 0.47 mN/m 
(CO2-NBW), representing 2.56 ± 1.40 %, 2.64 ± 1.19 %, and 2.10 ±
1.21 % reductions, respectively, versus the control (73.37 ± 0.77 
mN/m).
Digestate exhibits non-Newtonian fluid behavior, with viscosity 
primarily governed by substrate concentration, encompassing both 
soluble and insoluble fractions. As evidenced in Fig. 4, the apparent 
viscosity of digestate decreased with increasing rotational speed, 
demonstrating characteristic shear-thinning behavior consistent with 
documented rheological properties of anaerobic sludge [11]. During 
semi-continuous operation, viscosity progressed through three distinct 
phases: initial decline, subsequent increase, and eventual stabilization. 
Early-phase viscosity reduction (days 0–9) resulted from rapid microbial 
proliferation and discharge of startup-phase insoluble solids, coupled 
with accelerated consumption of soluble organics. This is in accordance 
with batch digestion systems, where a proportional decrease in viscosity 
was observed with a concomitant reduction in solids [38]. Subsequently, 
the substrate concentration within the digestate increased progressively 
until stabilization, resulting in a corresponding rise in viscosity to a 
steady-state value. Rheological measurements across varying rotational 
speeds demonstrated significantly lower apparent viscosity in 
NBW-supplemented groups compared to the control. This reduction 
primarily stems from NB-enhanced degradation of lignocellulosic sub­
strates, whereby NBW supplementation promoted microbial hydrolysis 
of solid fractions into soluble constituents. The viscosity-lowering effect

3.4. Microbial community structure
AD involves synergistic microbial consortia, with distinct community 
structures emerging across metabolic phases. The Shannon index and 
Simpson index are routinely employed to quantify microbial community 
diversity. An elevated Shannon index signifies greater community di­
versity, whereas the Simpson index exhibits an inverse relationship with 
diversity [39]. As presented in Table 2, archaeal diversity increased 
substantially after long-term digestion compared to the initial inocula, 
whereas bacterial diversity declined. This was due to the weak meth­
anogenic capacity of the inoculum in the early stage, and a single species 
of methanogens. In the later stage, with the increase of available sub­
strate, all kinds of methanogens reproduced in large quantities, ulti­
mately forming a stable and rich archaeal community structure. 
Notably, NBW-supplemented systems exhibited lower Simpson indices 
for both archaea and bacteria relative to controls. This reduction sig­
nifies NBW-mediated enrichment of microbial biodiversity, thereby 
augmenting functional redundancy within the anaerobic ecosystem.
Under fixed temperature, substrate composition, and operational 
conditions, AD systems exert a directional enrichment effect on micro­
bial consortia [40]. Compared to the initial inocula, long-term operation 
substantially altered dominant bacterial genera across all groups 
(Fig. 5). The control group developed DMER64 as the predominant 
genus, which is a propionate/butyrate-oxidising hydrogen producer 
capable of direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) with methanogens

N/S cycling maintains proton gradient equilibrium across cellular 
membranes, thereby sustaining system stability and metabolic efficiency 
[46]. This mechanistic alignment is evidenced by the documented ca­

swine manure digestion [47]. Additionally, CO2-NBW exhibited 
elevated expression of aromatic hydrocarbon degradation, ligninolysis, 
and xylanolysis genes. CH4-NBW demonstrated strengthened capabil­

3.6. Mechanism analysis
As illustrated in Fig. 9a, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) relaxa­
tion times were significantly prolonged in NBW compared to deionized 
water. The T2 relaxation time measured 2713.19 ms for deionized water 
versus 2870.47 ms (H2-NBW), 2804.70 ms (CH4-NBW), and 2946.07 ms 
(CO2-NBW). Extended relaxation times indicate enhanced water mo­
lecular mobility, which facilitates molecular diffusion and mass transfer 
processes [49]. In AD systems, the elevated mobility and diffusivity of 
NBW promote cellulose hydrolysis efficiency [27]. This hydrodynamic 
enhancement directly improves mass transfer kinetics, accelerating 
substrate flux and energy transduction [50]. Optimized mass transfer 
efficiency supports microbial metabolic activities, thereby increasing 
substrate utilization. In this research, NBs selectively enriched func­
tional microbial consortia, stimulating substrate degradation and 
methanogenic gene expression. This leads to substantial compositional 
changes in the digestate, thereby affecting its physicochemical proper­
ties. These effects include decreased viscosity and surface tension, as 
well as increased specific heat capacity. Therefore, under conditions of 
enhanced thermal stability and flow characteristics, microbial activity, 
mass transfer, and NBs become more stable.
In summary, NBW operates through synergistic heat-mass transfer 
and microbial mechanisms. By establishing a “mass transfer- 
microorganisms-thermophysical properties” positive feedback loop 
(Fig. 9b), comprehensive system enhancement was achieved. This 
enhancement was realized through four interconnected mechanisms: (1) 
enhancement of mass transfer efficiency; (2) selective microbial 
enrichment and functional amplification; (3) alteration of material flux 
and spatial distribution; (4) improvement of digestate flow properties 
and thermal stability. At the microbial level, the efficient mass transfer 
facilitated by NBW inevitably alters the microbial community structure 
and enhances metabolic activity. This represents the core mechanism of 
NBW’s effect. Concurrently, accelerated microbial metabolism improves 
substrate utilization efficiency, thereby altering substance concentra­
tions. These differing substance distribution patterns lead to variations 
in the physicochemical properties of the digestate, which indirectly in­
fluence its thermophysical properties. Ultimately, this creates a more 
stable environment for both AD microorganisms and NBs, fostering a 
robust “mass transfer-microbial activity-thermophysical properties” 
cycle within the system. While the inherent physicochemical properties

3.7. Energy efficiency analysis and outlook
The two primary sources of energy input involved in the application 
of NBs in AD are the electrical energy consumed by the operation of the 
nanobubble generator and the calorific value contained in the gas itself. 
However, due to limitations in current nanobubble detection techniques 
(such as nanoparticle interference and bubble stability), it is difficult to 
accurately determine the amount of gas dissolved in the liquid phase. 
Therefore, this paper only briefly discusses the energy efficiency rela­
tionship between the energy consumption for preparing NBW and the 
resulting energy gain. The calculation results show that under different 
conditions, the net energy ratios of the NBW groups are 0.42 (H2-NBW), 
0.32 (CH4-NBW), and 0.68 (CO2-NBW), respectively. As shown in 
Fig. 10, the net energy ratio is closely related to the circulation prepa­
ration time of NBW. As the circulation time increases, the net energy 
ratio gradually decreases. With a methane production rate increase of 
15.67 %, the net energy ratio reaches 1 when the circulation preparation 
time of CO2-NBW is 3.21 min. However, under conditions without cir­
culation preparation (t = 0.67 min), the net energy ratios for adding 
NBW are 3.13 (H2-NBW), 2.37 (CH4-NBW), and 5.07 (CO2-NBW), 
respectively. This indicates that in practical engineering applications, 
the circulation preparation time per unit volume of NBW should be 
minimized or circulation preparation should be avoided altogether to 
enhance the system’s energy efficiency.
The improvement of thermophysical properties of digestate by NBW 
suggests its significant potential in reducing energy consumption asso­
ciated with mixing and dynamic heating. Compared to traditional 
chemical additives, NBW does not require subsequent recovery and will 
not cause secondary pollution to the AD system, thereby further 
reducing its operational costs. Nevertheless, future studies should 
include a comprehensive life cycle analysis encompassing the gas pro­
duction stage to comprehensively evaluate its overall benefits. For other 
organic wastes (such as food waste, sludge, or agricultural residues), 
nanobubble technology also holds promise for enhancing overall system 
efficiency by improving mass and heat transfer and regulating microbial 
metabolism. It is particularly noteworthy that the NB-AD technology can 
be efficiently integrated with other bioenergy systems. For instance, it 
can be combined with biohydrogen production systems to convert a low 
concentration of hydrogen into NBW for enhancing the AD process, 
thereby improving overall energy recovery efficiency while reducing 
operational costs. Although the integration of nanobubble technology 
into existing biogas projects demonstrates good operational feasibility, 
its large-scale application still faces numerous challenges, including 
optimal dosing strategies and uniform distribution during continuous 
operation. Future research should focus on long-term performance 
evaluations at pilot scale, techno-economic analyses of the full life cycle, 
and detailed investigations into the interaction mechanisms between 
NBs and complex microbial communities.
4. Conclusion
This research evaluated the effects of NBW on semi-continuous AD, 
elucidating its enhancement mechanisms through thermophysical and 
microbial analyses. NBW demonstrated sustained performance 
improvement in corn stover digestion, with mean daily methane pro­
duction during stable operation increasing by 9.68 ± 2.08 % (H2-NBW), 
7.34 ± 2.07 % (CH4-NBW), and 15.67 ± 1.96 % (CO2-NBW) relative to 
the control. On one hand, NBW enhanced substrate degradation effi­
ciency, leading to improved removal rates of TS and VS. On the other 
hand, NBW accelerated the consumption of reducing sugars and SCOD 
while enhancing the VFAs generation rate. Concurrently, NBW effec­
tively improved the thermophysical properties of the digestate, thereby 
optimizing heat and mass transfer processes. Compared to the control, 
H2-NBW increased the specific heat capacity by 1.23 ± 0.33 % and 
decreased viscosity and surface tension by 11.13 ± 0.20 % and 2.56 ±
1.40 %, respectively. Furthermore, NBW enriched the microbial com­
munity diversity within the AD system, increasing the relative abun­
dance of various hydrolytic/acidogenic bacteria, as well as diverse 
methanogenic archaea. Both H2-NBW and CO2-NBW induced a shift in 
the methanogenic pathway towards hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. 
However, CH4-NBW led to the significant enrichment of nor­
ank_Bathyarchaeia, which consequently suppressed the functional 
expression of hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis. Collectively, these 
findings indicate that NBs operate through a synergistic mechanism 
involving enhanced heat-mass transfer and microbial community mod­
ulation, ultimately improving methane production efficiency and system 
stability.
